senses.gloss:
Nāyanārs
(‘lords,’ ‘servants of the Lord’)
------------------------------------------
The भक्ति Movement—the religious movement that upheld the superiority of भक्ति or devotion to God, as the simplest and the easiest mode of sādhanā or spiritual practice—saved हिन्दुइस्म् from the labyrinth of Vedic rituals and the Hindu society from being demographically wiped out.
The आऌवार्स् (Vaiṣṇava saints) and the नायनार्स् (also spelt as ‘Nāyanmārs’) (Śaiva saints), both belonging to the Tamil Nadu, were the leading lights of this movement in South India, during the period 7th and 8th centuries A. D.
The नायनार्स् are 63 in number. They came from all castes and all levels of the Hindu society and included quite a few women-saints too.
Their main contributions were: off-setting the effects and spread of जैनिस्म् and बुद्धिस्म् which had become more of a heretical movement than of true एथिच्स् and spiritual values; vigorously propagating the cult of devotion to God as शिव; transcending all social barriers brought about by caste, wealth or power, through devotion to God as the sole means of estimating the worth of a human being; and, development of chaste Tamil literature.
A comprehensive account of all the 63 नायनार्स् is given in the celebrated Tamil classic, the Periyapurāṇam of Sekkizhār (12th century A. D.), which contains 4000 verses.
The more important and better known नायनार्स् are: ज्ञानसम्बन्धर्, अप्पर् (or Tirunāvakkarasar). Sundara-mūrti and Tirunīlakaṇṭhar.
The philosophy and religion of the नायनार्स् was primarily based on the शैवसिद्धान्त.
The Tevāram, compositions of अप्पर्, सुन्दरमूर्ति and ज्ञानसम्बन्धर्, are chanted or sung in the शिव temples of Tamil Nadu even today.
The नायनार्स् advised their followers to give five kinds of gifts: आहार (food), bhaiṣajya (medical relief), abhaya (protection from fears and dangers), śāstra (religious instructions), and दान (presents of articles needed by the poor people).
In the राजराजेश्वरी temple of Tañjā-vūr, there are relief figures depicting some incidents from the lives of a few of these नायनार्स्. Their images are found in the Nañjuṇḍeśvara temple at Nañjanagūḍu in the Mysore district of Karnataka.
